sources.title: ViPRA: Video Prediction for Robot Actions

sectionsRead: Appendix C: Multimodal Video Pretraining with Latent Actions
Appendix D: Flow Matching Decoder for Continuous Control
Appendix E.1–E.4: SIMPLER and LIBERO Long
omissions: Text extraction does not reconstruct figure images; inspect the retained PDF for figures and equation/table layout.

Identity/version: the title and all five authors match the catalog. The inspected artifact is arXiv:2511.07732v2, dated 30 March 2026, and marked as published at ICLR 2026. The catalog BibTeX instead names NeurIPS Workshop, 2025; that earlier edition was not supplied or compared.
The supplied text extraction does not reconstruct figure images; original PDF pages and six final crops were inspected to recover visual and equation/table layout.
Separate supplemental material availability has not been fully verified.
All 11 supplied text chunks were read, covering the complete 36-page PDF. Visual inspection covered the claim-supporting pages declared in the edition; reference-list pages were read as text.
Code, external project material and rollout videos were not inspected; no experiments were reproduced.

synopsis: ViPRA learns discrete motion representations from actionless human and robot videos, jointly pretrains an LWM video-language backbone on future images and latent actions, then adapts that backbone to continuous action chunks. Its control policy does not generate future video at deployment. Gains on SIMPLER and physical manipulation coexist with weaker LIBERO-10 results and unresolved flow-matching notation (e-method, e-pretrain, e-adapt, e-simpler, e-real, e-libero, e-flow-convention).

problem.text: Passive videos show interactions without the robot commands needed for imitation learning. ViPRA asks whether predicting visual change and motion latents can supply transferable control priors, leaving a smaller labeled demonstration set to align those priors with a robot's motor space.

contributions.text: A non-causal inverse model learns discrete transition tokens through causal visual reconstruction, perceptual supervision and bidirectional optical-flow consistency.

A shared video-language transformer predicts an end-of-horizon image and the intervening latent-action sequence during pretraining; continuous finetuning then learns embodiment-specific action chunks.

inputs: Actionless human/robot clips and task descriptions for pretraining
Two observation frames and a language instruction for control
Labeled robot action chunks during adaptation
outputs: Future visual tokens and discrete motion latents during pretraining
Continuous robot action chunks during ViPRA-FM deployment

steps.name: Extract motion tokens
steps.detail: The DINOv2-initialized inverse encoder Iβ sees the entire clip, including future frames, and quantizes contextual features through NSVQ into a shared eight-entry codebook. The causal forward decoder Fα reconstructs each next frame from observation and latent histories. These training-time inferred latents are not measured robot commands.

steps.name: Learn visual and latent transitions together
steps.detail: Frozen VQ-VAE tokenization maps observations to visual tokens. LWM-Chat-1M, latent embedding Eϕ and token decoder Hψ are trained with teacher forcing. From history and language, the sequence predicts future image tokens before the latent tokens, which condition on that future image during training.

steps.name: Adapt the shared backbone to motors
steps.detail: A noisy-action encoder Eγ embeds the continuous action chunk and interpolation time; the backbone and flow head Hη predict its refinement field. Algorithm 3 updates all three components. Its conditioning contains history, language and noisy actions, with no explicit generated image or discrete-latent input.

training.text: Pretraining uses 198k Something-Something v2 human videos and actionless robot subsets of 87k Fractal, 25.4k BridgeV2 and 85.6k Kuka videos. Adaptation uses 100 collected multi-task SIMPLER trajectories; the physical single-arm study states 180 GELLO demonstrations per task.

Latent learning runs 240,000 steps, batch 128, with flow supervision after 60,000 steps. Multimodal pretraining runs 50,000 steps, batch 512, with H=14; SIMPLER flow adaptation uses 12,000 steps. The VQ tokenizer remains frozen, while the video backbone is trainable.

inference.text: The stated sampler uses ten forward Euler steps. Language/image KV states are cached across these steps. The physical single-arm protocol predicts 14 actions and executes seven before replanning from updated observations; it reports a capped effective rate of 3.5 Hz.

Future-image prediction is removed for action finetuning and control. Thus video modeling supplies learned priors rather than an online visual-planning loop. The inverse tokenizer labels training clips; it is not a runtime inverse model translating generated frames into commands.

equations.explanation: Equation (2): reconstruction uses pixel L1; LPIPS supplies perceptual similarity. Lflow compares RAFT flow in both temporal directions between reconstructed and observed frames. The indicator activates flow after warm-up αflow; weights are 0.5 for LPIPS and 0.1 for flow.

Equation (3): x denotes visual tokens, z latent-action tokens, hats predictions, CE cross-entropy, H the prediction horizon, and the two N terms the token counts. Both objectives train the same backbone.

As printed in Section 4.3: a is the demonstrated chunk, u0 Gaussian noise, s is sampled from Beta(1.5,1), and ĝ is the predicted field. The interpolation places actions at s=0 and noise at s=1, conflicting with the stated noise-to-action integration from 0 to 1. The intended convention remains unresolved.

results.setting: Four Bridge tasks on WidowX after 100 multi-task finetuning trajectories; success and grasp are separate metrics.
results.interpretation: AR exceeds LAPA by 16.7 percentage points; FM exceeds Scratch-FM by 20.8 points. This simulation ranking does not establish physical superiority of AR.

results.setting: Cover-Object, Pick-Place and Stack-Cups; fixed front camera, 180 demonstrations per task and seven-of-fourteen action execution.
results.comparison: Figure 3: π₀ 41.8 and Scratch-FM 23.8; Section 5.4 instead prints π₀ 40.1.
results.interpretation: The figure supports a 12.3-point advantage over π₀. The conflicting prose baseline is not silently reconciled. Trial counts and uncertainty are not given for this aggregate.

results.setting: Ten tasks, ten runs per task under five seeds: 500 episodes. Appendix E calls the aggregate average reward; Table 8 labels it success rate.
results.interpretation: Transfer is positive but not leading. Sensing differs across methods; the authors associate precision-grasp failures with accumulated delta-end-effector drift.

results.setting: Table 2, average SIMPLER success over four Bridge tasks, H=14.
results.value: Full AR/FM: 69.8/62.5; without pretraining state prediction: 59.4/53.2; without chunking: 59.2/44.8.
results.comparison: Moving state prediction into finetuning gives 53.1/31.3.
results.interpretation: Joint pretraining helps. The +SP3 rows also remove pretraining state prediction, so they do not isolate adding a finetuning loss while holding pretraining fixed.

results.setting: Human-only, robot-only and combined latent learning/pretraining, evaluated on LIBERO-10.
results.interpretation: Combining sources improves these reported measures; the table does not establish a data-volume-matched comparison.

results.setting: Latent learning with versus without optical-flow loss; frozen-backbone probe predicts BridgeV2 actions.
results.interpretation: The probe supports more action-informative representations. Lower token uncertainty alone does not prove physical correctness or better executed control.

results.setting: Two Franka arms, single front camera, shared policy, 14-action chunks at stated 7 Hz.
results.comparison: No quantitative bimanual baseline is supplied.
results.interpretation: Demonstrates coordinated execution in these setups; the authors attribute bowl-task failures mainly to grasping limitations of the custom gripper.

limitations.text: The authors identify limited data diversity, dexterous contact control and unknown scaling behavior as open problems. Test-time planning and reinforcement-learning alignment are future directions, not evaluated capabilities.

Smoothness figures replay finetuning trajectories through the inference pipeline; they are qualitative diagnostics, not held-out jerk statistics. Baselines vary in pretraining data, architecture and action space, limiting causal attribution of the headline gains.

The reported 510 ms per 14-action chunk and approximately 1.95 chunk predictions/s do not mean 22 fresh visual decisions/s. Appendix G's 3.5/7 Hz rollout terminology does not fully specify the scheduler or reconcile robot-side execution with replanning.

reproduction.text: Required components include LWM-Chat-1M, its VQ tokenizer, DINOv2, RAFT, the four video sources and downstream demonstrations. Tables 5–6 report eight NVIDIA H100 GPUs for 168 hours of latent learning and 144 hours of pretraining. Section 7 claims released code/models but describes the collected SIMPLER trajectories as a future release.

Before reproducing control, resolve the contradictory flow endpoints and field scaling in Section 4.3, Equations (7)–(10) and Algorithm 3. Also specify action normalization, dataset splits, software versions, physical-trial counts and timing hardware: these are not sufficiently pinned down by the supplied configuration tables and evaluation descriptions.

reasoning.text: The recorded One Model × Joint prediction classification is supported for pretraining: a single shared transformer produces future visual tokens and latent actions through modality heads. Separate training tokenizers do not turn this into a deployed video-generator-plus-inverse-controller pipeline. Qualify the label at inference: ViPRA-FM emits continuous actions without joint future-video prediction.

discussionQuestions: Would the pretraining advantage survive matching video volume, compute, sensing and action parameterization across baselines?
How much of observed retry behavior depends on temporal pretraining versus observation history and action-chunk execution?

evidence.location: PDF p. 1, title block, arXiv margin and Abstract
evidence.detail: Title and five authors match the supplied identity; affiliations are Carnegie Mellon University, Skild AI and University of California, Irvine. Margin states arXiv:2511.07732v2, 30 March 2026; header names ICLR 2026.

evidence.location: PDF p. 4, Figure 2 and Section 4.1
evidence.detail: Three-stage architecture; inverse encoder uses full observation clips and an eight-entry shared codebook.

evidence.location: PDF p. 5, Section 4.1, Equations (1)–(2)
evidence.detail: Causal reconstruction uses L1, LPIPS and two-direction RAFT flow consistency activated after warm-up.

evidence.location: PDF p. 23, Appendix B and Algorithm 1; p. 24, Figure 7
evidence.detail: DINOv2-initialized spatial encoding, bidirectional inverse temporal attention, NSVQ and causal forward temporal attention define latent learning.

evidence.location: PDF p. 5, Section 4.2 and Equation (3); p. 25, Algorithm 2
evidence.detail: LWM jointly trains visual and latent token predictions with teacher forcing; latent prediction conditions on end-of-horizon visual tokens.

evidence.location: PDF p. 24, Table 5, Training Configuration and Latent Action Quantization
evidence.detail: 240,000 steps, batch 128, 60,000-step flow warm-up, LPIPS/flow weights 0.5/0.1, eight H100 GPUs for 168 hours; codebook size eight.

evidence.location: PDF p. 26, Table 6
evidence.detail: Frozen VQ-VAE, trainable LWM and latent modules; 50,000 steps, batch 512, H=14, AdamW at 4e-5, bfloat16; eight H100 GPUs for 144 hours.

evidence.location: PDF p. 6, Section 4.3; p. 27, Algorithm 3 and Table 7
evidence.detail: Continuous adaptation updates backbone, noisy-action encoder and flow decoder; Beta(1.5,1) interpolation, H=14 and ten Euler steps; SIMPLER uses 12,000 steps.

evidence.location: PDF p. 6, Section 4.3 interpolation and inference paragraph; pp. 21–22, Equations (7)–(10); p. 27, Algorithm 3 lines 2–7
evidence.detail: Printed interpolation weights noise by s and target by 1-s, but the sampling description calls s=0 noise and s=1 target. The objective scales predicted field by 1-s while Euler integration uses the field directly.

evidence.location: PDF p. 6, Section 5.1, Training Dataset, Simulation Benchmarks and Real World Manipulation
evidence.detail: Lists 198k human videos; 87k Fractal, 25.4k BridgeV2 and 85.6k Kuka videos; 100 collected SIMPLER trajectories and 180 physical demonstrations per task.

evidence.location: PDF p. 7, Table 1, Success Rates and Grasp Rates, AVG and task rows
evidence.detail: Average success: ViPRA-AR 69.8, ViPRA-FM 62.5, LAPA 53.1, OpenVLA 38.6, Scratch-FM 41.7, π₀ 27.1, UniVLA 42.7. UniVLA per-task entries are absent.

evidence.location: PDF p. 28, Appendix E.1–E.2
evidence.detail: Four Bridge tasks, WidowX, 100 collected multitask adaptation trajectories; separates complete task success from successful grasp.

evidence.location: PDF p. 7, Figure 3, Full and Partial panels; p. 8, Section 5.4
evidence.detail: Figure average full success is 54.1 for ViPRA-FM, 41.8 for π₀ and 23.8 for Scratch-FM; prose instead gives π₀ 40.1. Figure shows Cover-Object partial/full ViPRA values 98.1/59.2 and no error bars.

evidence.location: PDF p. 7, Section 5.1 continuation below Table 1
evidence.detail: Front camera, full versus grasp success definitions, H=14, seven executed actions before replanning and stated 3.5 Hz evaluation cap.

evidence.location: PDF p. 7, Section 5.2
evidence.detail: Baseline families differ in backbone, action representation and pretraining sources; UniPI/VPT results are taken from prior work in a stated comparable setting.

evidence.location: PDF p. 9, Table 2, Pretrain/Finetune/Succ. columns; pp. 8–9, Section 5.5
evidence.detail: Full AR/FM 69.8/62.5; −SP2 59.4/53.2; −AC 59.2/44.8; +SP3 53.1/31.3. The +SP3 rows train latent-only before adding future-state prediction at finetuning.

evidence.location: PDF p. 9, Table 3; p. 10, Human and robot data composition ablation
evidence.detail: Combined, robot-only and human-only success/MSE: 0.79/0.84, 0.72/0.91, 0.69/0.99; task is LIBERO-10.

evidence.location: PDF p. 9, Table 4; p. 10, Latent action analysis
evidence.detail: With/no flow: perplexity 5.01/5.63, entropy 1.59/1.74, action MSE 0.84/0.92. Text identifies a frozen-backbone BridgeV2 action probe.

evidence.location: PDF p. 9, Figure 6; p. 10, Section 5.5 continuation; pp. 30–31, Appendix F and Figure 8
evidence.detail: Blue ViPRA-FM traces are smoother than green LAPA traces in joint space. The diagnostic replays finetuning training trajectories through the inference pipeline; physical safety-stop observations are separate author reports.

evidence.location: PDF p. 29, Table 8 and Appendix E.3–E.4
evidence.detail: LIBERO-10 uses 500 episodes; ViPRA-FM 0.79 trails π₀ 0.85, UVA 0.90 and UniVLA 0.92. Text discusses image-only sensing and delta-EEF drift.

evidence.location: PDF p. 32, Appendix G.1–G.3; p. 33, Figure 9 and G.4
evidence.detail: Two Franka Panda arms, one front-mounted ZED camera used monocularly, GELLO collection at 15 Hz; object/cloth/cup changes and qualitative retries are described.

evidence.location: PDF pp. 33–34, Appendix G.5 and Table 9
evidence.detail: Image/language KV reuse across Euler steps; 14-action chunk in 510 ms, about 1.95 Hz. Text separately reports 7/14 and 14/14 rollout rates of 3.5 and 7 Hz and robot-side rates up to 22 Hz; table identifies ViPRA as 7B.

evidence.location: PDF p. 35, Appendix H.1 and Figure 10; p. 36, H.2 and Figure 11
evidence.detail: Shared policy coordinates both Franka arms from one camera; stated 14-action chunks at 7 Hz. Place-in-Bowl completes 10/18 and Mix-with-Whisk 8/12 trials.

evidence.location: PDF p. 10, Section 6
evidence.detail: Limits include dexterity, dataset diversity and uncharacterized scaling; tactile/force sensing, broader embodiments, RL alignment and planning are proposed directions.

evidence.location: PDF p. 11, Section 7
evidence.detail: Names open components and claims released code, models and benchmark scripts, while describing the collected SIMPLER dataset release in future tense.
